text: GlideRecord is ServiceNow's server-side API for working with table data, and it's the single most load-bearing API in the whole platform. In this lesson, we're looking at what it actually is before we touch any methods.

Creating a GlideRecord doesn't load anything. Writing new GlideRecord, passing in the table name incident, just creates a cursor — an object positioned over the incident table's schema, not a copy of its data. Nothing hits the database yet. GlideRecord is a cursor, able to point at zero, one, or many rows one at a time, and you decide when it actually asks the database a question.

The simplest thing you can do with that cursor is retrieve exactly one record by a value you already know identifies it uniquely — almost always the sys_id. Calling get with a sys_id returns true if a match was found, positioning the cursor on it, or false if nothing matched. Inside the if block, getValue of number reads a field off the record GlideRecord just found.

GlideRecord isn't one option among several — it's the foundation nearly everything else in server-side scripting sits on. A Business Rule hands you current, which is a GlideRecord already positioned on the record that triggered it. A Script Include method that needs data creates its own GlideRecord to query something. A Scheduled Job that sweeps through stale records — closing old requests, say — uses GlideRecord to find and loop through them.

Here's the fact that makes Business Rules click into place: current, inside a Business Rule, is literally a GlideRecord object, already queried and positioned on the one record being inserted, updated, or deleted. In this before-update rule on incident, current.priority and current.state are read directly, and current.work_notes is set directly — exactly the same dot-notation field access you'll use on any GlideRecord you create yourself.

A GlideRecord is a cursor, not a loaded record, and current in a Business Rule is one you were handed for free. Next lesson, we build the real querying pattern — addQuery, query, and the while loop that walks through every matching row.
